name: Mustarde otoplasty

lead: The Mustarde technique is a way of pinning back prominent ears. A surgeon places mattress sutures through the back of the ear to fold the cartilage into a natural antihelix, the Y-shaped ridge inside the rim, which brings the outer rim closer to the head.

For appearance, the goal is ears that sit flatter and look proportionate. It was introduced in 1963 and is widely used, often in children, with published series reporting good aesthetic results and a low complication rate.

paras: It is performed by a plastic or ENT surgeon, usually through an incision behind the ear, with sutures that reshape the cartilage without cutting it. It is often combined with other steps, such as conchal setback sutures or scoring of the cartilage. After surgery patients typically wear a dressing and then a headband, particularly at night, for several weeks.

Reported complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion and overcorrection, with one clinical trial citing complications in up to 25% of otoplasties overall. Techniques differ in revision rates and results depend on the surgeon. It is a surgical procedure and should be discussed with a qualified clinician.

chain: Ear rim sits closer to the head
Ears look flatter and more proportionate
angle.text: The procedure reshapes the ear's contour so prominent ears lie flatter. This directly changes how the ears look, which patients often cite as a confidence matter.

lead: The Mustarde technique is an otoplasty method for correcting prominent ears. Mattress sutures placed on the back of the ear fold the cartilage to form the antihelix, which pulls the helical rim back toward the head without reshaping the cartilage itself. It was described by J. C. Mustarde in 1963.[1]

People pursue it to get ears that sit closer to the skull and look more balanced with the face. Prominent ears are common, with one report putting prominauris at 5% of the population, and the associated psychological burden, including teasing in childhood, is a frequently cited reason for correction.[2][3]

Clinical literature includes case series and comparisons. A 2020 review of patients under 18 described the Mustarde otoplasty as 'good-fast-cheap', and a 2011 Spanish series reported good aesthetic results in all patients with a low complication rate.[4][5]
infobox: Permanent mattress sutures on the back of the ear

paras: Mustarde's technique belongs to the group of otoplasty methods that keep the cartilage intact and use sutures to fold it. In the open version, the cartilage at the back is widely exposed and a strip of skin removed before the sutures are tightened.[1]

Surgeons frequently combine it with other steps. A 2021 randomized trial used Stenstrom's anterior cartilage scoring together with Mustarde's technique as its base approach.[6] A 2025 paediatric series modified it with an instrument-guided fold and Furnas sutures for conchal setback.[2]
Operations can be outpatient. A loose dressing is worn for several days, followed by a snug headband worn at night for roughly three to six weeks so the ears do not fold forward in sleep.[1]

A 1986 retrospective survey of 191 patients under 16 compared the Mustarde technique with anterior scoring and found no difference in final acceptance between the two methods.[7] A 2025 series of 35 paediatric patients reported significant pre- to post-operative differences in measured auricular points.[2]
Reviews describe overcorrection, an unnaturally pinned look, as the most significant aesthetic complication.[1]

Reported complications include hematoma needing prompt drainage, infection including perichondritis, suture extrusion behind the ear with granuloma, and overcorrection.[1] The 2021 trial notes that up to 25% of otoplasties can have complications.[6]

Mustarde also described flap designs for epicanthal folds, and the name appears in eyelid-surgery literature, including studies in children with Down syndrome and blepharophimosis.[8] This is a different procedure from the otoplasty technique.

A 2021 randomized controlled trial of 42 patients compared needles with rasps for cartilage scoring combined with Mustarde sutures, assessing anatomical and aesthetic endpoints and complications.[6] A retrospective 1986 study compared Mustarde with anterior scoring in 191 patients.[7] A 2020 retrospective study examined efficacy, safety and resource use of the Mustarde otoplasty in patients under 18.[4] A 2011 evaluation reported good aesthetic results in all patients.[5]
